blocks.text: The key benefit of Zero Trust Browser is that it provides users with the ability to access the internet within Chromium-based browsers that are in a sandboxed environment. The temporary format of this container is made possible by the idle timeout restriction, which causes the isolated browser to expire and close after 10 minutes of user inactivity. By default, all the data in that expired isolated browser is purged, along with all the isolated web content and the associated state. However, admins can enable a persistent state of the isolated browser. To ensure an intuitive browsing experience, isolation profiles with this feature enabled have sessions restored automatically upon user access.

To allow users to access this feature, admins must enable the Persistent State setting on the user's isolation profile. To learn more, see Creating Isolation Profiles for Internet & SaaS and Creating Isolation Profiles for Private Access.

To initiate the persistent state feature for the isolation session, the user clicks the refresh button for the URL from within the isolated container. The browser then refreshes the URL and restarts the isolated session. If the user begins a brand-new isolation session, this action restores the user's authentication state for apps and browsing history from their last session. The only time it does not refresh the existing information is if this feature has been disabled for the user's isolation profile between the old and new session.

The persisting session information is backed up in an encrypted state to the Zscaler cloud. If the session with the persisting data is not restored for 15 days, the data is purged permanently. As soon as you disable persistent state for a user, their persisting session data is also purged. Persistent session data cannot exceed 100 MB. To learn more, see Ranges & Limitations.
If a user attempts to restore a session three or more times without success, or the restored browser does not load, have them contact their Zero Trust Browser admin.
